briefing:
SITUATION BRIEFING — Round 5

It is Day 2, 10:00 CET. NATO has delivered a 24-hour ultimatum: Russia must begin withdrawal by 08:00 Day 3 or face military action.

MILITARY: OPLAN BALTIC SHIELD approved — SEAD phase begins after ultimatum expires.
- Phase 1: 48-72h SEAD campaign to destroy S-400/EW
- Phase 2: Ground assault — Polish 18th Mech from south, German 45th from north
- Phase 3: Stabilization
Russian response: additional Iskander-M forward, second S-400 activated, fortifications hardening. Supply lines vulnerable — single rail from Belarus, one road from Kaliningrad.

FORCES: Polish 18th Mech at assembly areas. V Corps combat-ready. German 45th at Rukla. UK 4th Brigade moving south from Estonia. French 11th Para en route. Finnish arty committed. Ford CSG ETA ~18h. Dutch 43rd preparing. Italian Cavour preparing. 3 Russian subs in Norwegian Sea.

CYBER: Russian Sandworm attacked Polish railway (contained in 3h). Estonian CCDCOE counter-op degraded Russian EW briefly.

DIPLOMATIC: Ultimatum delivered 08:00 CET. Russia calls it 'hysterical,' invokes nuclear doctrine. Kremlin summons NATO ambassadors. Belarus signals non-involvement through Kellogg channel. India/China call for restraint.

ECONOMIC: Oil $105. Markets down 8% from pre-crisis. Saudi signals 300K bpd spare capacity but conditions on F-35 deal.

NUCLEAR: Iskander-M launchers moved forward in Kaliningrad. Could carry nuclear warheads. Russian nuclear posture remains 'elevated.' No warhead mating detected.

CRITICAL: The ultimatum expires at 08:00 Day 3. Russia will NOT withdraw. SEAD operations will begin. This is the last 22 hours before combat between NATO and Russian forces.
narrative:
The early morning hours of Day 2 belonged to the generals. At SHAPE headquarters in Mons, SACEUR General Grynkewich presented his operational concept to the North Atlantic Council at 06:00 CET. The plan, designated OPLAN BALTIC SHIELD, was a phased approach: Phase 1 would be a 48-72 hour Suppression of Enemy Air Defense (SEAD) campaign using F-35s from Lakenheath, EA-18G Growlers from the Ford CSG (now 18 hours out), and allied Eurofighters and Rafales to destroy or degrade the S-400 batteries covering the corridor. Phase 2 would be a ground assault led by the Polish 18th Mechanized Division from the south and the German 45th Panzer Brigade from the north, supported by US V Corps artillery and Finnish long-range fires. Phase 3 would be corridor stabilization and permanent garrison.

The political debate that followed was brutal. Poland demanded immediate action — '24 hours lost is 24 hours Russia uses to dig in deeper.' Lithuania's representative was emotional, citing Sergeant Kavaliauskas's capture. But the US position, delivered by Rubio, was firm: Washington would authorize SEAD operations only after a 24-hour diplomatic window during which a formal ultimatum would be delivered to Moscow: withdraw from the corridor within 48 hours or face military expulsion. The compromise was painful but held.

At 08:00 CET, NATO Secretary General delivered the ultimatum publicly. Russia had until 08:00 on Day 3 to begin verifiable withdrawal. The 24-hour clock was ticking.

Russia's response came within the hour. Foreign Minister Lavrov dismissed the ultimatum as 'hysterical' and announced that Russia would 'defend its humanitarian corridor with all available means, consistent with our nuclear doctrine.' The Kremlin summoned ambassadors from NATO frontline states and delivered a chilling message: 'Any attack on Russian forces in the corridor will be treated as an attack on Russian sovereign territory. Consider the implications carefully.'

Behind the rhetoric, Russia was preparing. In Kaliningrad, additional Iskander-M launchers — capable of carrying either conventional or nuclear warheads — were moved to forward positions visible to NATO satellites. A second S-400 battery was activated, creating overlapping kill zones across the entire corridor. Engineers worked through the night on concrete-reinforced positions. But critically, Russian supply lines were already strained — the corridor depended on a single rail line from Belarus and one road from Kaliningrad, both vulnerable to interdiction.

The cyber front escalated dramatically. At 04:30 CET, GRU Unit 74455 (Sandworm) launched a coordinated attack against Polish railway management systems, temporarily disrupting signaling on the Białystok-Suwałki line — the key NATO logistics artery. The attack was detected within 40 minutes and contained within 3 hours, but it demonstrated Russia's ability to strike at NATO's supply chain. Estonia's CCDCOE responded with a counter-cyber operation that reportedly degraded Russian electronic warfare coordination in the corridor for several hours.

Other developments added layers of complexity. Norway reported that the Yasen-class submarine had been joined by two Severodvinsk-class boats — three nuclear-capable submarines now operating in the Norwegian Sea, the largest Russian submarine deployment since the Cold War. Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi placed an emergency call demanding that no Pacific assets be transferred to Europe. Ukraine intensified deep-strike operations inside Russia, hitting an ammunition depot in Smolensk Oblast that intelligence suggested was staging supplies for the corridor.

surprises: At 09:50 CET, the German Bundestag's intelligence committee chair received a classified briefing revealing that German BND intercepted a conversation between General Lapin (Russian Western Military District) and a Kaliningrad garrison commander in which Lapin was heard saying: 'The corridor is a political gesture, not a military position. We cannot hold it against a serious NATO assault. Tell Moscow the truth before they get us all killed.' The intercept, shared with SACEUR, fundamentally shaped the military assessment that Russia's defensive position was weaker than it appeared — the troops in the corridor knew they were expendable.
